sets.title: Management History
sets.desc: Questions 1–40: 24 multiple choice (five options) and 16 true or false, as in the 2017 final.

qs.q: The Egyptian pyramids and the Great Wall of China are used in management history to show that:
o: scientific management began in ancient times
projects of tremendous scope, employing tens of thousands of people, were completed in ancient times
bureaucracy was first designed in Egypt
machine power replaced human power long before the industrial revolution
ancient builders worked without any form of planning or control

qs.q: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith argued for the economic advantages of:
The industrial revolution is best described as a period when:
o: machine power was substituted for human power, making it more economical to manufacture goods in factories than at home
skilled artisans replaced machines in most factories
managers first applied statistics to military problems
organizations began to be viewed as open systems
quality experts introduced continuous improvement in Japan

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four major approaches to management theory?
The classical approach to management emphasized:
o: the external environment of the organization
rationality and making organizations and workers as efficient as possible
matching management style to the situation

qs.q: Scientific management involves using the scientific method to:
o: find the "one best way" for a job to be done
respond to customer needs and expectations

qs.q: A supervisor at a bottling plant times each task with a stopwatch, replaces workers' rule-of-thumb methods with a studied method, and then selects and trains workers to follow it. The supervisor is applying the ideas of:
Which of the following is NOT one of Taylor's four principles of scientific management?
o: Develop a science for each element of an individual's work.
Scientifically select and then train, teach, and develop the worker.
Heartily cooperate with the workers so that work is done in accordance with the science developed.
Divide work and responsibility almost equally between management and workers.
Allow workers to choose their own work methods and train themselves as best they can.

qs.q: Therbligs are:
o: a classification scheme for labeling basic hand motions
the written rules of a bureaucracy
statistical techniques used in quality management
the inputs an open system takes from its environment

qs.q: Henri Fayol based his management theory on his personal experience as:
o: a first-line supervisor at Midvale Steel
the managing director of a large French coal-mining firm
a quality consultant to Japanese manufacturers

qs.q: Which of Fayol's principles states that every employee should receive orders from only one superior?
A manager organises team-building days because she believes that promoting team spirit builds harmony and unity in the organization. Which of Fayol's principles is she applying?
Weber's bureaucracy is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
o: selection of people based on friendship and family ties

qs.q: A government office applies its rules and controls in exactly the same way to every employee, regardless of who they are. Which characteristic of Weber's bureaucracy does this illustrate?
Organizational behavior (OB) is:
o: the use of quantitative techniques to improve decision making
a form of organization with detailed rules and regulations
the breakdown of jobs into narrow and repetitive tasks
the study of the actions of people at work
a set of interrelated and interdependent parts

qs.q: Which early advocate of OB was a pioneer of industrial psychology and suggested using psychological tests for employee selection?
Who was the first to argue that organizations were open systems?
Which of the following was NOT one of the four early advocates of the OB approach?
The Hawthorne Studies concluded that:
o: group standards establish individual worker output
money is the main factor in determining output
individual behavior is unaffected by group factors
there is one best way to do every job

qs.q: The quantitative approach to management evolved from:
o: Adam Smith's writings on division of labor
mathematical and statistical solutions developed for military problems during World War II

qs.q: Total quality management (TQM) is a philosophy of management driven by:
o: continuous improvement and responsiveness to customer needs and expectations
finding the one best way to do each job
matching the leader's style to the situation
keeping the organization closed to its environment

qs.q: An organization that takes in resources from its environment, transforms them, and distributes outputs back into the environment is described as:
The contingency approach says that:
o: there is one best way to manage all organizations
organizations should avoid interacting with their environment
people are the least important asset of an organization
management principles can be applied in all organizational situations
organizations are different, face different situations, and require different ways of managing

qs.q: A structure that works well for a company of 50 employees proves inefficient when the company grows to 50,000 employees. Which contingency variable does this illustrate?
Frederick W. Taylor is known as the "father" of scientific management.
Fayol developed 14 principles of management that he believed could be applied in all organizational situations and taught in schools.
Weber believed that his "ideal bureaucracy" existed in most organizations of his time.
Division of labor is also known as job specialization.
Robert Owen argued that money spent improving labor was a smart investment.
The Hawthorne Studies were conducted by Hugo Munsterberg.
The Hawthorne Studies found that money is a greater factor in determining output than group standards, group attitudes, and security.
The quantitative approach is also known as management science.
In total quality management, the term "customer" refers only to outsiders who buy the organization's products or services.
The ideas of W. Edwards Deming and Joseph M. Juran were enthusiastically embraced by Japanese organizations before Western managers took them seriously.
Closed systems are influenced by and interact with their environment.
The contingency approach is sometimes called the situational approach.
The primary value of the contingency approach is that it gives managers simple, universal rules to follow.
Fayol's principle of remuneration states that workers must be paid a fair wage for their services.
In Weber's bureaucracy, managers are the owners of the units they manage.
Mary Parker Follett thought that organizations should be based on a group ethic.

sets.title: Foundations of Planning
sets.desc: Questions 41–80: 24 multiple choice (five options) and 16 true or false, as in the 2017 final.

qs.q: Planning is the management function that involves:
o: arranging and structuring work to accomplish goals
influencing a group to achieve goals
setting goals, establishing strategies for achieving those goals, and developing plans to integrate and coordinate work activities
energizing, directing, and sustaining employee effort

qs.q: Planning is concerned with both:
Which of the following is NOT a feature of formal planning?
o: Goals cover a specific time period.
Goals are shared with organizational members.
Goals are kept in the manager's head to keep them flexible.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons managers plan?
o: Planning establishes the goals and standards used in controlling.
Planning eliminates change in the environment.

qs.q: After a factory coordinates its work activities around a plan, managers notice that two departments have been doing the same checks, and they remove one. Which purpose of planning does this illustrate?
Research suggests that at least ____ years of formal planning are required before it begins to affect performance.
In studies where formal planning did not lead to higher performance, the culprit was often:
Plans are best defined as:
o: official statements of what the organization wants the public to believe
documents that outline how goals are going to be met
visual representations of an organization's structure
data that managers use to make strategic decisions

qs.q: Plans that apply to the entire organization and establish the organization's overall goals are called:
Long-term plans are plans with a time frame:
Short-term plans are plans covering:
o: any period chosen by top management

qs.q: A manager's plan states: "Cut costs by 4 percent and increase revenue by 6 percent within six months." It leaves no room for interpretation. This is a:
Plans that are flexible and set out general guidelines are called:
A university draws up a plan for hosting its once-off 50th anniversary celebration. This plan is a:
Standing plans include:
Which of the following is a contingency factor that affects planning?
o: the manager's level in the organization

qs.q: When an organization's environment is highly uncertain and likely to change, its plans should be more:
Lower-level managers focus mostly on _ planning, while top executives focus mostly on _ planning.
A company's website says its top priority is protecting the environment, but its actions show it is mainly pursuing higher profits. Higher profits are the company's ____ objective.
In traditional objective-setting:
o: employees and managers jointly agree on goals
top managers set objectives that flow down through the organization and become subgoals for each organizational area
lower-level employees set the goals for top managers
goals are set by an outside consultant

qs.q: A common problem with traditional objective-setting is that:
o: clarity is lost as objectives make their way down from the top of the organization to lower levels
employees participate too much in setting goals
goals become too specific at the top
performance feedback is given too often
top managers have no say in the goals

qs.q: Management by objectives (MBO) is:
o: an approach in which top managers alone set goals
a one-time plan designed for a unique situation
screening information to detect emerging trends
a process of setting mutually agreed-upon goals and using those goals to evaluate employee performance
a system for sharing financial statements with employees

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four elements of an MBO program?
o: goals imposed by top management without discussion

qs.q: Gathering information about competitors that allows managers to anticipate competitors' actions rather than merely react to them is called:
Planning eliminates uncertainty.
Doing a good job of planning and implementing the plans plays a bigger part in high performance than how much planning is done.
Goals are also called objectives.
Strategic plans are narrow, while operational plans are broad.
A plan covering a period between one year and three years would be an intermediate plan.
Directional plans lock managers into specific goals and courses of action.
Strategic plans are usually long-term, directional, and single use.
An organization's stated objectives are always the same as its real objectives.
MBO uses goals to motivate employees, not only to check that they are doing what they are supposed to do.
When the environment is highly uncertain, managers should stop formal planning.
To plan effectively in dynamic environments, lower organizational levels should be allowed to set goals and develop plans.
Environmental scanning is screening information to detect emerging trends.
Well-written goals are measurable, quantifiable, and clear as to time frame.
Well-written goals should be easy enough for every employee to reach without effort.
Business intelligence refers to the technology, systems, or software that allow the user to collect, visualize, understand, or analyze data.
Virtual reality is a three-dimensional, interactive, computer-generated experience that occurs within a simulated environment.

sets.title: Organizing
sets.desc: Questions 81–120: 24 multiple choice (five options) and 16 true or false, as in the 2017 final.

qs.q: Organizing is the management function that involves:
o: arranging and structuring work to accomplish the organization's goals
influencing a group to achieve goals
screening information to detect emerging trends

qs.q: The visual representation of an organization's structure is called:
Which of the following is NOT one of the six key elements of organizational design?
Temporary, freelance, or contract workers whose employment depends on demand for their services are called:
When work specialization is carried too far, human diseconomies appear. These include all of the following EXCEPT:
A plant manager has five managers reporting to her: engineering, accounting, manufacturing, human resources, and purchasing. This plant uses ____ departmentalization.
A retailer has one sales director for the northern region, one for the southern region, and one for the western region. This is an example of ____ departmentalization.
A bank has separate managers for retail accounts, wholesale accounts, and government accounts. This is an example of ____ departmentalization.
A disadvantage of process departmentalization is that it:
o: can only be used with certain types of products
gives a limited view of organizational goals
leaves units feeling isolated from other organizational areas
produces poor communication across functional areas

qs.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of functional departmentalization?
o: it can only be used with certain types of products
poor coordination within the functional area

qs.q: A work team composed of individuals from various functional specialties is called a:
The line of authority extending from upper organizational levels to the lowest levels, which clarifies who reports to whom, is the:
Authority that entitles a manager to direct the work of an employee is called:
A hospital administrator cannot handle the purchasing of all supplies, so she creates a purchasing department to support and advise her. The purchasing department holds:
The obligation or expectation to perform any assigned duties is called:
The number of employees a manager can efficiently and effectively manage is the:

Two organizations each have about 4,100 employees. One has a span of control of four and the other a span of eight. The organization with the wider span will have two fewer levels and approximately ____ fewer managers.
The degree to which decision making is concentrated at upper levels of the organization is called:
More decentralization is appropriate when:
o: the organization is facing a crisis or the risk of company failure
lower-level managers do not want a say in decisions
the environment is complex and uncertain

qs.q: Formalization refers to:
o: the basis by which jobs are grouped together
the degree to which lower-level employees make decisions
how standardized an organization's jobs are and the extent to which employee behavior is guided by rules and procedures
the number of levels in the organization
the visual representation of the structure

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of an organic organization?
According to Woodward's findings, the most effective structure for mass production technology is:
A unique aspect of the matrix structure is that it:
o: creates a dual chain of command
is made up entirely of contingent workers
concentrates all authority in one person

qs.q: Employees at a firm must work 40 hours a week and be present between 10:00 and 14:00, but may choose their own starting and finishing times. This arrangement is called:
A virtual organization consists of a small core of full-time employees and outside specialists temporarily hired as needed to work on projects.
Job sharing is the practice of having two or more people split a full-time job.
The traditional view was that managers could not, and should not, directly supervise more than five or six subordinates.
The trend in recent years has been toward smaller spans of control.
An organization is either completely centralized or completely decentralized.
Employee empowerment means giving employees more authority to make decisions.
In highly formalized organizations, employees have a great deal of discretion over what is done, when it is done, and how it is done.
A mechanistic organization is highly adaptive and flexible.
An organic structure works well for an organization pursuing meaningful and unique innovations, while a mechanistic structure works best for companies wanting to tightly control costs.
Large organizations, typically those with more than 2,000 employees, tend to have more specialization, departmentalization, centralization, and rules than small organizations.
Woodward found that an organic structure is most effective with unit production and process production technology.
The greater the environmental uncertainty, the more an organization needs a mechanistic design.
A simple structure has little departmentalization, wide spans of control, centralized authority, and little formalization.
A weakness of the divisional structure is that duplication of activities and resources increases costs and reduces efficiency.
In a project structure, employees return to their formal departments when a project is completed.
In a compressed workweek, employees work fewer hours per day but more days per week.

sets.title: Leadership
sets.desc: Questions 121–160: 24 multiple choice (five options) and 16 true or false, as in the 2017 final.

qs.q: A leader is best defined as someone who:
o: owns the unit he or she manages
has technical skills but no authority
can influence others and who has managerial authority
dictates work methods and limits participation

qs.q: Leadership is:
o: a process of influencing a group to achieve goals
the formal arrangement of jobs within an organization
the obligation to perform assigned duties
the set of rules that guide employee behavior
a document that outlines how goals will be met

qs.q: Leadership research in the 1920s and 1930s that tried to isolate leader traits found that:
o: physical stature always separates leaders from nonleaders
social class is the best predictor of leadership
leaders are born with seven fixed traits
fluency of speech is the only trait that matters
it was impossible to identify a set of traits that would always differentiate a leader from a nonleader

qs.q: Leaders who build trusting relationships with followers by being truthful and by showing high consistency between word and deed are displaying which trait?
In the University of Iowa studies, a leader who dictates work methods, makes unilateral decisions, and limits employee participation uses the ____ style.
Mpho lets her team make all the decisions and complete the work in whatever way they see fit. According to the University of Iowa studies, Mpho's style is:
The two dimensions of leader behavior identified by the Ohio State studies were:
o: concern for people and concern for production

qs.q: A supervisor is friendly and approachable, helps group members with personal problems, and treats all group members as equals. In the Ohio State studies, this supervisor is high in:
The University of Michigan studies concluded that:
o: production-oriented leaders achieved the highest satisfaction
employee-oriented leaders were able to get high group productivity and high group member satisfaction
the autocratic style was most effective
a leader's style cannot be measured
leaders should match their style to follower readiness

qs.q: The managerial grid appraises leadership styles using which two dimensions?
o: concern for people and concern for production

qs.q: On the managerial grid, a leader with a high concern for people and a low concern for production (1,9) uses:
The Fiedler contingency model proposes that effective group performance depends on:
o: the leader removing roadblocks from the followers' path
the proper match between a leader's style and the degree to which the situation allows the leader to control and influence

qs.q: The least-preferred coworker (LPC) questionnaire measures:
o: the level of trust in a work group
whether a leader is task oriented or relationship oriented

qs.q: Fiedler's three situational contingency dimensions are:
o: leader-member relations, task structure, and position power

qs.q: According to Fiedler, task-oriented leaders perform best in situations that are:
Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership theory (SLT) focuses on:
A new group of trainees is motivated but lacks the appropriate skills (unable but willing). According to SLT, the leader should use the ____ style.
A team of experienced engineers is both able and willing to do what is asked of them. According to SLT, the leader should use the ____ style.
Path-goal theory was developed by:
In path-goal theory, a leader who sets challenging goals and expects followers to perform at their highest level is:
The leadership theory that says leaders create in-groups and out-groups, and that those in the in-group will have higher performance ratings, less turnover, and greater job satisfaction, is:
Leaders who guide or motivate followers toward established goals by exchanging rewards for their productivity are called:
Employees follow a manager's instructions because they fear he will suspend or demote them. The manager is using:
Junior staff admire Ms. Dube, want to be associated with her, and want to be like her. The power Ms. Dube holds over them is:
Managers should be leaders because leading is one of the four management functions.
The University of Iowa researchers' results indicated that the autocratic style contributed to both good quantity and quality of work.
A leader high in both initiating structure and consideration always achieves high group task performance and high group member satisfaction.
Although the managerial grid has 81 potential categories, only five styles were named.
Fiedler assumed that a leader's style was fixed.
According to Fiedler, relationship-oriented leaders perform better in moderately favorable situations.
In situational leadership theory, readiness refers to the extent to which people have the ability and willingness to accomplish a specific task.
The telling style is low task–high relationship.
House assumed that leaders are inflexible and cannot change their leadership behavior.
Path-goal theory takes key elements from the expectancy theory of motivation.
A charismatic leader is an enthusiastic, self-confident leader whose personality and actions influence people to behave in certain ways.
Servant leaders put their own needs ahead of the needs of their followers.
Legitimate power and authority are the same.
Expert power is the power a leader has as a result of his or her position in the organization.
Of the five dimensions of trust, integrity seems to be the most critical when someone assesses another's trustworthiness.
Follower characteristics such as experience, training, and professional orientation can act as substitutes for leadership.

sets.title: Motivation
sets.desc: Questions 161–200: 24 multiple choice (five options) and 16 true or false, as in the 2017 final.

qs.q: Motivation is:
o: the way tasks are combined to form complete jobs
an individual's belief that he or she is capable of performing a task
the perceived fairness of the allocation of rewards
the process by which a person's efforts are energized, directed, and sustained toward attaining a goal
the degree of control employees have over their work

qs.q: The three key elements in the definition of motivation are:
Which of the following lists Maslow's needs in the correct order, from lowest to highest?
Thabo's main concern at work is having job security and protection from physical and emotional harm. According to Maslow, which need is Thabo trying to satisfy?
A person's needs for affection, belongingness, acceptance, and friendship are:
An accountant works hard mainly because she wants status, recognition, and attention from others. According to Maslow, she is motivated by:
Theory X is the assumption that employees:
o: are motivated only by intrinsic factors
dislike work, are lazy, avoid responsibility, and must be coerced to perform
compare their inputs and outcomes with those of others

qs.q: A manager gives her staff responsible and challenging jobs and involves them in decision making because she believes they enjoy work and seek responsibility. She holds ____ assumptions.
According to Herzberg, which of the following is a motivator?
According to Herzberg, when hygiene factors are adequate, people will be:
o: not dissatisfied, but not satisfied (or motivated) either

qs.q: According to Herzberg, the opposite of "satisfaction" is:
The three-needs theory was proposed by:
The need to make others behave in a way that they would not have behaved otherwise is the:
According to the three-needs theory, the best managers tend to be:
o: high in the need for affiliation and low in the need for power
high in the need for power and low in the need for affiliation
high in the need for affiliation and high in the need for power
low in the need for power and low in the need for affiliation

qs.q: Goal-setting theory proposes that:
o: easy goals produce higher performance than difficult goals
general goals produce higher performance than specific goals
goals have no effect on performance
behavior is a function of its consequences
specific goals increase performance, and difficult goals, when accepted, result in higher performance than easy goals

qs.q: An individual's belief that he or she is capable of performing a task is called:
The theory that behavior is a function of its consequences is:
A receptionist who used to only answer phones is now also asked to file documents, sort the mail, and book meeting rooms. Her job has been horizontally expanded. This is:
Job enrichment is the vertical expansion of a job by adding planning and evaluating responsibilities. It increases:
Which of the following is NOT one of the five core job dimensions in the job characteristics model (JCM)?
In the job characteristics model, autonomy leads to which critical psychological state?
o: experienced responsibility for outcomes of the work
knowledge of the actual results of the work activities

qs.q: In equity theory, the persons, systems, or selves against which individuals compare themselves to assess equity are called:
Kabo is certain that if he reaches his sales target, he will receive the bonus his manager promised. In expectancy theory, this belief is:
A motivational approach in which an organization's financial statements are shared with all employees is called:
High levels of effort always lead to favorable job performance.
Maslow argued that each level in the needs hierarchy must be substantially satisfied before the next need becomes dominant.
Theory Y is a negative view of people.
Herzberg's two-factor theory is also called motivation-hygiene theory.
According to Herzberg, removing dissatisfying characteristics from a job will necessarily make that job more satisfying.
The three needs in McClelland's three-needs theory are innate rather than acquired.
The needs for achievement, power, and affiliation can be measured using the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT).
In difficult situations, people with low self-efficacy are likely to reduce their effort or give up altogether.
Reinforcement theory focuses on goals, expectations, and needs.
Job depth is the degree of control employees have over their work.
Task identity is the degree to which a job has a substantial impact on the lives or work of other people.
Distributive justice is the perceived fairness of the amount and allocation of rewards among individuals.
Valence is the importance an individual places on the potential outcome or reward that can be achieved on the job.
Expectancy theory was developed by Victor Vroom.
Most current motivation theories were developed in the United States by Americans and about Americans.
Money and promotions are typically at the top of the list of what motivates professionals.
